src: Peer-reviewed papers (Nature, Science, PNAS, PLoS ONE, Antiquity), Smithsonian, Science Museum Group, British Museum, British Library, UNESCO, NASA, IEEE Milestones, Library of Congress, US National Park Service, museums named per entry
fmt: [year, event title, lat, lon, kind, one line, Wikipedia title, source, place, card name, 1 = adds facts to an event already in the timeline]
inv: The oldest known stone tools are knocked out at Lomekwi
Cores and flakes about 3.3 million years old, older than the genus Homo.
Oldowan choppers and flakes are made at Gona
Sharp flakes struck from river cobbles, the start of the long-lived Oldowan toolkit.
The first Acheulean hand axes are shaped at Kokiselei
Teardrop-shaped hand axes worked on both faces, a design used for over a million years.
Notched logs are joined into a wooden structure at Kalambo Falls
Two interlocking logs shaped with stone tools, the oldest known woodworking structure.
Hunters carve wooden throwing spears at Schöningen
Spruce and pine spears about 2 m long, found with butchered horses by a lakeshore.
Conard et al. 2020, Nature Ecology & Evolution
An ochre paint workshop is set up in Blombos Cave
Two abalone shells used as paint pots, with grinders and ochre mixed with bone fat.
Pierced shell beads are strung in Blombos Cave
Tick-shell beads with drilled holes and wear from string, among the oldest known jewellery.
Engraved ostrich-egg water flasks are made at Diepkloof
Eggshell containers engraved with repeated line patterns, used to carry water.
Ground-edge stone axes are hafted in the Kimberley
A fragment of a ground-edge axe about 45,000 to 49,000 years old, the oldest known.
Bone flutes: the first known musical instruments
A vulture-bone flute with five finger holes from Hohle Fels Cave.
Ivory carvings like the Lion-man figurine
A 31 cm lion-headed figure carved from mammoth ivory.
Wild flax fibres are spun and dyed at Dzudzuana Cave
Twisted and dyed flax fibres about 30,000 years old, for cords and cloth.
The Venus of Dolní Věstonice is among the oldest fired ceramics.
Wild cereals are tended and ground at Ohalo II
A lakeshore camp with grinding stones and early trial cultivation of wild barley and wheat.
Pottery sherds from Xianrendong Cave about 20,000 years old.
Charred bread crumbs about 14,400 years old, baked by hunter-gatherers before farming.
Clovis spear points spread across North America
Fluted stone points made for a few centuries around 13,000 years ago.
Wooden boomerangs are carved at Wyrie Swamp
Returning and non-returning boomerangs preserved in peat about 10,000 years old.
Luebbers 1975, Archaeology & Physical Anthropology in Oceania
A stone tower rises at Jericho
An 8.5 m stone tower with an inner staircase, one of the oldest known monumental buildings.
Barkai and Liran 2008, Cambridge Archaeological Journal
The Pesse canoe is hollowed from a pine log
A 3 m dugout canoe about 10,000 years old, the oldest known boat.
A pine dugout canoe is paddled at Kuahuqiao
A canoe about 8,000 years old, found with paddles in a Neolithic village.
Banana and taro gardens are drained at Kuk Swamp
Ditches and mounds show farming began independently in the New Guinea highlands.
Copper is smelted from ore at Belovode
Slag about 7,000 years old, the oldest secure evidence of copper smelting.
Radivojević et al. 2010, Journal of Archaeological Science
Gold is worked into jewellery at Varna
Graves with over 3,000 gold objects, the oldest processed gold yet found.
Silk fabric fragments about 5,600 years old from a Yangshao village.
A cowhide shoe is laced at Areni-1
A one-piece leather shoe about 5,500 years old, the oldest known.
The Tarkhan dress is sewn from linen
A pleated linen shirt about 5,100 years old, the oldest known woven garment.
UCL Petrie Museum; Stevenson and Dee 2016, Antiquity
Writing: cuneiform in Sumer, hieroglyphs in Egypt
Clay tablets from Uruk record grain, beer and workers.
British Museum; Metropolitan Museum of Art
Merer writes a logbook on papyrus at Wadi al-Jarf
The oldest inscribed papyri: a work diary of hauling limestone for the Great Pyramid.
The Khufu ship is built and buried at Giza
A 43 m cedar ship found in pieces in a pit beside the Great Pyramid.
Miners write the first alphabet at Serabit el-Khadim
Proto-Sinaitic letters borrowed from hieroglyphs, ancestor of most alphabets.
Rubber balls are made at El Manatí
Solid rubber balls about 3,600 years old, made by mixing latex with morning-glory juice.
Scribes write a 30-letter alphabet in Ugarit
Wedge-shaped cuneiform letters, one sign per sound.
Oracle bones carry the first Chinese writing at Anyang
Shang kings asked questions of ancestors on cracked turtle shells and ox bones.
Phoenician letters are carved at Byblos
A 22-letter alphabet, spread by traders, became Greek, Latin and Arabic letters.
The Diolkos paved trackway hauls ships across the Isthmus of Corinth
A stone road with grooves for wheeled trolleys carrying ships between two seas.
Lydian coins of electrum, stamped with a lion's head.
The Persian Royal Road links Susa to Sardis
A 2,700 km highway with relay stations; couriers crossed it in about 9 days.
Iron is smelted on a large scale at Meroë
Slag heaps around the Kushite capital show a big iron industry.
The Appian Way is paved south from Rome
The first long Roman road, built by Appius Claudius, later reaching Brindisi.
Aqua Appia, Rome's first aqueduct, carries water into the city
A 16 km mostly underground channel bringing spring water to Rome.
The Dujiangyan irrigation system tames the Min River
A weir and channel system without dams that still waters the Chengdu Plain.
The Lingqu Canal joins the Yangtze and Pearl river systems
One of the oldest contour canals, built for the Qin armies heading south.
The Antikythera mechanism: an ancient computer
A bronze geared device that predicted eclipses, found in a shipwreck.
National Archaeological Museum, Athens; Freeth et al. 2006, Nature
Chinese ships steer with a sternpost rudder
A Han-dynasty pottery ship model from a Guangzhou tomb shows a rudder at the stern.
Guangzhou Museum; Needham, Science and Civilisation in China
Cai Lun reported paper made from bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets.
Book of the Later Han; British Library
A bronze jar whose dragons dropped a ball toward a distant earthquake.
Book of the Later Han; China Earthquake Administration
The Sui Grand Canal links north and south China
A canal network over 2,000 km long, dug in a few years to move grain to the capital.
The Diamond Sutra scroll from the Mogao Caves, printed from wood blocks.
The Song government prints the first official paper money
Jiaozi notes, first printed by Sichuan merchants, became a state currency.
Bi Sheng prints with movable clay type
Separate baked-clay characters set in an iron frame, described by Shen Kuo.
Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays; British Library
A magnetised fish compass points south
The Wujing Zongyao describes a heated iron fish floated on water to find south.
Su Song's water-driven astronomical clock tower runs in Kaifeng
A 12 m tower with an escapement turning an armillary sphere and a star globe.
Al-Jazari writes the Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
Water clocks, pumps and automata, with a crankshaft and segmental gears.
A friar preached in 1306 that spectacles had been invented about 20 years before.
Giordano da Pisa sermon; Museum of the History of Science, Florence
King Sejong proclaims the Hangul alphabet
A 28-letter alphabet designed so ordinary people could read and write Korean.
Gutenberg prints with metal movable type in Mainz
A press with cast metal type and oil ink; his Bible followed about 1455.
The Inca road network spans the Andes
Over 30,000 km of paved roads, stairways and rope bridges across the Andes.
Lippershey seeks a patent for a spyglass
A Middelburg spectacle maker asked the Dutch States General for a patent on a telescope.
The Pascaline added and subtracted with geared wheels, to help his tax-collector father.
A pendulum regulated clock, accurate to about a minute a day.
Abraham Darby smelts iron with coke at Coalbrookdale
Coke from coal replaced charcoal, making cheap iron possible.
Steam engines pump water from mines
Newcomen's atmospheric engine pumped water from a coal mine.
John Kay patents the flying shuttle
A shuttle thrown by a cord let one weaver make wide cloth twice as fast.
Hargreaves' frame let one worker spin eight threads at once.
Cugnot's steam carriage moves under its own power
A three-wheeled steam tractor built to haul cannon, the first self-propelled road vehicle.
James Watt patents the separate condenser
Keeping the cylinder hot cut the coal a steam engine burned by about three quarters.
Arkwright opens a water-powered cotton mill at Cromford
The first successful water-powered cotton spinning mill and a model for factories.
The Iron Bridge is raised over the Severn
The first major bridge made of cast iron, spanning 30 m.
People fly in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon
Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes floated about 9 km over Paris.
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
A loom driven by a machine instead of a weaver's hands and feet.
Eli Whitney builds the cotton gin
A toothed drum pulled cotton fibre from seeds, which spread slave-grown cotton farming.
Volta's pile of zinc and copper discs gave the first steady electric current.
Trevithick's locomotive hauls iron at Penydarren
The first steam locomotive to pull a load on rails, 10 tons of iron.
Jacquard's loom weaves patterns from punched cards
Chains of punched cards chose which threads to lift, an idea later used in computing.
Musée des Tissus de Lyon; Science Museum Group
Fulton's Clermont ran up the Hudson from New York to Albany in 32 hours.
A rolled paper tube, then a wooden one, to listen to the heart and lungs.
Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first train on the Stockton and Darlington Railway.
Niépce's view from a window took hours to expose on a pewter plate.
View from the Window at Le Gras
Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas
View from the Window at Le Gras
Faraday turned a copper disc between magnet poles to make current.
Cooke and Wheatstone's needle telegraph ran along a London railway.
The SS Great Britain is launched
Brunel's iron-hulled, screw-driven steamship, the first of its kind to cross the Atlantic.
Morse sends "What hath God wrought" from Washington to Baltimore
The first long-distance message on an American telegraph line.
Ether was used for a public operation at Massachusetts General Hospital.
The Crystal Palace is built of iron and glass
A 564 m hall of standard prefabricated parts, built in months for the Great Exhibition.
Bessemer blew air through molten iron to burn out carbon.
Drake drilled 21 m to strike oil in Pennsylvania.
The Metropolitan Railway ran steam trains under London streets.
A telegraph cable links Europe and America for good
The Great Eastern laid a lasting cable from Valentia, Ireland, to Heart's Content.
Nobel soaked nitroglycerin into clay to make it safer to handle.
The first transcontinental railroad is completed at Promontory Summit
A golden spike joined the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines.
The Sholes and Glidden typewriter goes on sale
Built by Remington, it introduced the QWERTY keyboard.
Bell spoke the first words by telephone to his assistant Watson.
Edison recorded "Mary had a little lamb" on tinfoil.
US National Park Service (Thomas Edison NHP)
A carbon filament bulb burned for over 13 hours at Menlo Park.
US National Park Service (Thomas Edison NHP)
Pearl Street Station lights lower Manhattan
The first central power station selling electricity to customers.
The Rover safety bicycle is built
Two equal wheels and a chain drive gave the modern bicycle shape.
The Home Insurance Building used a steel and iron frame to carry its walls.
Benz patented his three-wheeled Motorwagen with a petrol engine.
Made for his son's tricycle, it quickly spread to bicycles and cars.
Röntgen saw rays pass through flesh and photographed his wife's hand bones.
The Lumière brothers showed films to a paying audience in a Paris café.
The Wright Flyer flew 12 seconds and 37 m at Kill Devil Hills.
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, is made
A heat-set plastic from phenol and formaldehyde, used for radios and phones.
The Ford Model T, first built at the Piquette Avenue plant.
A moving assembly line builds cars at Highland Park
Ford cut the time to build a Model T chassis from about 12 hours to 1.5 hours.
Goddard launches the first liquid-fuel rocket
It flew for 2.5 seconds and rose about 12 m in a farm field.
Baird showed moving television pictures to scientists in Soho.
Radio echoes from a bomber were detected near Daventry.
Whittle's first jet engine ran on a test bed at Rugby.
Chicago Pile-1 under the stands of a football field went critical.
US Department of Energy; University of Chicago
Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley made the point-contact transistor at Bell Labs.
Bell Labs makes the first practical silicon solar cell
About 6% efficient, it soon powered satellites.
Obninsk fed 5 megawatts into the grid.
The Ideal X carries the first shipping containers
58 metal boxes sailed from Newark to Houston, starting container shipping.
A 58 cm metal ball that beeped by radio for three weeks.
Kilby builds the first integrated circuit
Several parts made on one piece of germanium: the microchip.
Tokyo to Osaka at up to 210 km/h, the first high-speed rail line.
ARPANET sends its first message between UCLA and Stanford
The network that grew into the internet; the first try crashed after "LO".
The Boeing 747 jumbo jet first flies
The first wide-body airliner, able to carry about 400 people.
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
A supersonic airliner that crossed the Atlantic in about 3.5 hours.
A whole computer processor on one chip, with 2,300 transistors.
Martin Cooper called a rival from a Motorola handset on Sixth Avenue.
A barcode is scanned at a checkout for the first time
A pack of chewing gum at Marsh Supermarket was the first UPC scan.
The first GPS satellite is launched
Navstar 1 began the 24-satellite Global Positioning System.
Tim Berners-Lee proposed linked hypertext documents at CERN.
Launched by the Space Shuttle Discovery from Kennedy Space Center.
The first text message is sent
An engineer sent "Merry Christmas" from a computer to a Vodafone phone.
Its first module, Zarya, was launched from Baikonur.
The iPhone was shown on stage in San Francisco.
A Falcon 9 booster lands back after an orbital launch
The first orbital rocket stage to land upright, making reuse possible.
An Ariane 5 rocket launched it from French Guiana.
A tokamak to test fusion power, built by 35 countries; dates in the 2024 baseline.
